PETITION FOR Review of Refund for Corporate Net Income Tax
PERIOD(S) 12/31/2009
AND NOW, May 20, 2014, pursuant to the Fiscal Code, the Act of 1929, April 9, P.L. 343,
as amended, (72 P.S. § 1 et seq), the Board of Finance and Revenue of the Commonwealth of
Pennsylvania, based upon the reasons set forth herein, hereby ORDERS the following:
Jurisdiction
This matter is before the Board of Finance and Revenue pursuant to Section 2704 of
the Tax Reform Code of 1971, as amended, 72 P.S. § 9704.
Issues
1. Whether the Board of Appeals correctly dismissed Petitioner’s refund case filed with
a debit balance in the 2009 corporate net income tax account?
2. Whether the Board of Appeals should have also dismissed Petitioner’s refund case
for lack of jurisdiction because it was filed more than three years after the tax payment due
date?
Statement of the Case
Petitioner, a Delaware corporation engaged in leasing commercial real estate, requests
that the Board of Finance and Revenue grant a refund by reducing Petitioner’s taxable income,
apportionment and corporate net income tax, but the instant matter was filed at the Board of
Appeals (BOA) with a debit balance in Petitioner’s 2009 corporate net income tax account and
it was filed more than three years from the tax payment date.
Petitioner had not made any payments, nor did Petitioner transfer credits to pay 2009
corporate net income tax.

On October 15, 2010, Petitioner filed a 2009 corporate report with the Pennsylvania
Department of Revenue claiming a $ corporate net income tax liability. Petitioner’s did not
pay any tax with the report filing and has not paid corporate net income tax to date. The
original return due date was April 15, 2010.
On May 15, 2013, the Department sent Petitioner a notice of audit assessment for a
$ corporate net income tax plus interest. The basis of assessment pertained to
decreases to the property, payroll and sales factor denominators, an increase in Federal
taxable income and a decrease of the net loss deduction to the $ statutory limit. The
Department of Revenue mailed a copy of its official notice of audit assessment to Petitioner
(Christos Vorillas) at 800 Long Ridge Road, Stamford, Connecticut (same address as given on
the BOA petition, BF&R petition and the tax return). The assessment notice contained the
following directions:
To appeal the assessment amount(s) above, file a petition for
reassessment with the Board of Appeals on or before
08/13/2013.
The assessed tax has never been paid.
On August 12, 2013, Petitioner filed a timely appeal of the assessment by petition for
reassessment (Docket No. 1316173) and the instant refund claim (Docket No.1316175) at the
Board of Appeals.
The Board of Appeals (or BOA) denied the net loss deduction and the various income
and apportionment claims in the petition for reassessment for a lack of sufficient details and
evidence but granted increases to Petitioner’s property and sales factor denominators for
Petitioner’s interest in a limited liability company.
The BOA dismissed this refund case for lack of jurisdiction due to nonpayment. The
$ audited and assessed corporate net income tax was not paid. This decision was
mailed to Petitioner on September 25, 2013.
The Board of Appeals mailed Petitioner the partial grant of the petition for reassessment
claims on November 27, 2013.
On December 19, 2013, Petitioner filed the instant review of refund claim at the Board
of Finance and Revenue requesting reduction of its 2009 corporate net income tax based on a
variety of taxable income, net loss deduction, apportionment factor, special apportionment,
nonbusiness income and multiform/unrelated income claims.
By letter dated March 13, 2014, Board counsel contacted Petitioner concerning the BOA
dismissal in this case for lack of payment and late filing and requested an explanation.

Petitioner’s counsel responds by letter dated March 24, 2014, arguing that the refund
was timely filed within three years of the extended filing date and within six months of an audit
assessment.
Petitioner reasons that an appeal period could not have started running without a return
filed. Petitioner did not file until October 15, 2010, and the August 12, 2013 Board of Appeals
filing date was within three years of the extended return filing and timely under 72 P.S. §
10003.1(a).
Petitioner claims that it timely filed for refund at the Board of Appeals on August 12,
2013, which was within six months of the May 15, 2013 audit assessment notice and timely
under 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b).
Petitioner adds that the refund claims were filed to preserve issues not listed on the
Basis of Assessment.
Statement of the Law
Our Supreme Court has held that limitations periods are absolute conditions to a right to
obtain relief. Federal Deposit Ins. Corp. v. Board of Finance and Revenue, 368 Pa. 463, 469-
470, 84 A.2d 495, 498-499 (1951). In any case, equitable principles cannot vary the statutory
time requirements. See, e.g., Bethlehem Steel Co. v. Board of Finance and Revenue, 431 Pa.
1, 10, 244 A.2d 767, 772 (1968) and Cooper v. Commonwealth, 700 A.2d 553, 554-555 (Pa.
Commw. 1997).
For a tax collected by the Department of Revenue, a taxpayer who has actually paid
tax, interest or penalty to the Commonwealth or to an agent or licensee of the Commonwealth
authorized to collect taxes may petition the Department of Revenue for refund or credit of the
tax, interest or penalty. Except as otherwise provided by statute, a petition for refund must be
made to the department within three years of actual payment of the tax, interest or penalty.
72 P.S. § 10003.1(a).
The department may grant a refund or credit to a taxpayer for all tax periods covered by
departmental audit. If a credit is not granted by the department in the audit report, the
taxpayer must file a petition for refund for taxes paid with respect to the audit period within six
months of the mailing date of the notice of assessment, determination or settlement or within
three years of actual payment of the tax, whichever is later. 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b).
In the case of amounts paid as a result of an assessment, determination, settlement or
appraisement, a petition for refund must be filed with the department within six months of the
actual payment of the tax. 72 P.S. § 10003.1(d).
A taxpayer shall be deemed to have timely filed a petition for resettlement, a petition for
reassessment, a petition for redetermination or any other protest relating to the assessment of
tax or any other matter relating to any tax imposed by this act if the letter transmitting the
petition is received by the Department of Revenue or is postmarked by the United States

Postal Service on or prior to the final day on which the petition is required to be filed.
72 P.S. § 10003.6.
Except as otherwise provided by this act, in all cases of petitions filed pursuant to this
article, the burden of proof shall be upon the petitioner or appellant, as the case may be.
72 P.S. § 9705.
Every petition . . . filed with the Board shall set forth the facts and points of law on which
the Petitioner relies. Any evidence in support of the petition shall be submitted simultaneously
with the petition or as promptly as possible thereafter. All evidential material shall be
submitted prior to five working days of the hearing date. 61 Pa. Code § 701.3(c).
Conclusion
The BOA correctly dismissed a refund case filed with a debit balance for the audited
and assessed tax in the tax account, but this refund was also filed more than three years after
the tax payment date.
The BOA only has jurisdiction to decide the merits of those refund cases concerning
money paid to the Commonwealth and filed within three years of the actual payment date or
within six months of an audit assessment. See 72 P.S. § 10003.1(a) and (b). The wording of
the statutes require refund claim amounts to have been paid as well as filing within the
prescribed deadlines. The three year provision in 72 P.S. § 10003.1(a) applies to “. . . a tax
collected by the Department of Revenue, a taxpayer who has actually paid tax,” which
indicates that payment is a requirement for a refund filing. Similarly, 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b)
refers to “filing claims for taxes paid with respect to the audit period,” which also indicates tax
payment is required for a refund claim.
A debit tax balance in Petitioner’s account without payment of that tax balance indicates
that Petitioner did not meet the threshold requirement of a refund claim—that the refund must
concern amounts paid to the Commonwealth. Not only did Petitioner not pay the tax balance
at the time of filing, but the claim was filed late.
Although Petitioner filed for refund within six months of the audit assessment, Petitioner
never paid any portion of the assessed tax and failed to meet the threshold payment
requirement included in 72 P.S. § 10003.1(b).
Petitioner did not report any corporate net income tax on the originally filed return, nor
did Petitioner pay the assessed tax. The instant refund claim is dismissed.
Petitioner’s arguments concerning the filing of the instant refund to preserve claims
outside the bases of assessment are not persuasive because Petitioner never paid the
reported tax and refund cases can only concern monies actually paid to the Commonwealth.
Accordingly, Petitioner’s refund request was correctly dismissed at the Board of Appeals
for lack of jurisdiction.
